newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan 1997 gold savings seen above 40 tonnes--WGC.
newsitem.headline: Japan 1997 gold savings seen above 40 tonnes--WGC.

text.p: Japanese investor purchases of gold in calendar 1997 through gold savings accounts are likely to surpass the previous year's 40 tonnes, the World Gold Council (WGC) said on Wednesday.
WGC also said the number of gold savings accounts in Japan will continue to rise, aided by Japan's "Big Bang" financial reforms.
Japanese investors bought 10.1 tonnes of gold through so-called gold accumulation plans in the January-to-March quarter this year, the WGC said.
"The main reason for this growth is the rising number of financial institutions offering such schemes," said Koichiro Kamei, manager of the information and planning department at WGC's Japan office.
Kamei said he expected Japanese investors to buy around 42 tonnes of gold this year, as the recent rise of the yen against the dollar, which lowered yen-based gold prices, may help boost gold demand.

"With the approach of the 'Big Bang' reforms, financial institutions will need to establish fee-based businesses. With tough competition likely, more financial institutions will offer (gold accumulation) schemes," Kamei said.
In 1996, Japan's gold investment demand was estimated at about 90 tonnes, down sharply from 180 tonnes in 1995 due to the yen's weakness against the dollar.
The total number of such accounts at the end of March this year was 720,000, up from 700,000 at the end of 1996 and 630,000 at the end of March last year, WGC said.

Under the accumulation plans, each month investors deposit a minimum of 3,000 yen in an account, which is used to purchase gold. The institution handling the account will generally buy some gold each day, aiming to get the best price for that day.
Payments are automatically transferred from the investors' bank accounts and they can usually choose to exchange the gold for cash, gold jewellery or gold bars.
Gold accumulation schemes are offered by Japanese bullion houses and most city banks. One city bank and several regional banks began offering such schemes this year, Kamei said.
